name: Lip scrub (exfoliation)

card.summary: Abrasive scrub for flaky lips; no studies, and dermatologists describe exfoliation as optional.
card.note: Overuse can irritate the skin barrier.

quick.overview:
A lip scrub uses abrasive grains to rub off flakes from the lips. It is a kind of mechanical exfoliation.

No studies of lip scrubs were found.
quick.mechanism: Abrasives physically remove surface skin cells.
quick.risks: Dermatologists quoted on Wikipedia say over-exfoliating can weaken the skin barrier and cause redness and sensitivity.

lead: A lip scrub is an abrasive product, commonly sugar- or salt-based, used to rub flaking skin off the lips. People use it to get smoother, softer-looking lips so that lip balm, lipstick or gloss goes on evenly, and to remove visible flakes that can make the lips look dry or uneven.[1][3]

It is a form of mechanical exfoliation, in which abrasives such as sugar or salt crystals, cloths or brushes physically remove surface skin cells; the alternative is chemical exfoliation with acids or enzymes.[1] Lip skin is thin, with only about three to five cell layers compared with up to 16 in facial skin, and has no hair and no sweat glands, which is why lips dry out and chap more easily than other skin.[4]

Dermatologists quoted on Wikipedia say manual or chemical exfoliation is not medically necessary because skin sheds dead cells on its own, and that overdoing it can weaken the skin barrier and cause sensitivity and redness.[1] Wikipedia's article on cheilitis lists lip licking and weather as common causes of chapped lips and describes barrier lubricants such as lip balm or petroleum jelly as the usual treatment.[2][3]

chain: Abrasive scrub lifts flaking surface skin
Lip surface looks smoother and softer
Balm or lipstick applies more evenly on a smoother base
angle.text: A scrub removes visible dry flakes, so the lips look smoother straight afterwards and take colour or balm more evenly. The effect is cosmetic and lasts as long as the lips stay hydrated.

infobox: About 3 to 5 cell layers; no hair or sweat glands[4]

paras: Mechanical exfoliation uses abrasives such as microfiber cloths, scrubs, crushed shells, sugar or salt crystals, pumice, sponges, loofahs and brushes. Chemical exfoliation uses alpha hydroxy acids such as glycolic and lactic acid, beta hydroxy acids such as salicylic acid, or enzymes to loosen dead cells.[1] Lip scrubs belong to the mechanical group, and some products pair the abrasive with oils or butters.

Lips lack sweat glands and the oil layer that normally keeps skin smooth, so they dry and chap quickly.[4] Wikipedia's lip balm article lists cold, dry or windy weather, lip licking and mouth breathing as causes of chapping, and says balms form an occlusive layer that seals in moisture.[3] Common balm bases include beeswax, candelilla and carnauba wax, lanolin and petrolatum.[3]

sections.h: Use in looksmaxxing and appearance routines
paras: Lips matter to appearance because the red vermilion zone and the Cupid's bow define the lower face, and Wikipedia's lip article notes survey-based links between lip fullness and attractiveness while flagging the sourcing as weak.[4] Lip scrubs fit into the broader lip-care routine of scrub, balm and colour.[3][4]
A T Nation poster describes lips that 'never heal' and develop a layer of dead skin that has to be removed, an example of the dry-lip complaint that scrubbing is meant to address.[5]

Over-exfoliation of skin is described as capable of impairing the barrier and increasing tightness, sensitivity, dryness and infection risk.[1] In exfoliative cheilitis, a rare condition with scaling lips, a link to lip picking or licking habits has been reported.[2]
